issues.legal_issue: A High Court may interfere in supervisory review with an inferior tribunal’s findings only where the tribunal’s decision is affected by a manifest error or comparable defect, rather than merely because the High Court would reach a different view of the evidence.
material_facts: The appellate authority reversed the Rent Controller’s findings on habitual default and subletting.

The High Court found that the appellate authority had misconstrued the agreement concerning the premises and had reached a conclusion on habitual default that was inconsistent with the material before it.
The High Court restored the Rent Controller’s permission to determine the tenancy on the grounds of habitual default and subletting.

The Supreme Court considered the challenge to the High Court’s exercise of supervisory jurisdiction and held that it had corrected errors in the appellate authority’s decision rather than impermissibly acting as an appellate court.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in interfering with the appellate authority’s findings because those findings involved manifest errors, including misconstruction of a document; the High Court did not exceed the limits of its supervisory jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution, the High Court exercises supervisory, not appellate, jurisdiction and cannot simply reconsider the correctness of an inferior tribunal’s decision. It may interfere where the tribunal has manifestly misconstrued documents, reached a conclusion no reasonable person could reach on the material, ignored relevant material, or relied on inadmissible material. No earlier case is relied on in the Court’s reasoning on this principle.

rule.if: supervisory_review_of_inferior_tribunal_order and (tribunal_misconstrued_material_document or tribunal_reached_unreasonable_conclusion or tribunal_ignored_relevant_material or tribunal_relied_on_inadmissible_material)

predicates.supervisory_review_of_inferior_tribunal_: A party challenged an inferior tribunal’s order in a proceeding invoking the High Court’s supervisory jurisdiction.
predicates.tribunal_misconstrued_material_document: The inferior tribunal construed a document material to its decision incorrectly.
predicates.tribunal_reached_unreasonable_conclusion: The inferior tribunal reached a conclusion on the material that a reasonable decision-maker could not reach.
predicates.tribunal_ignored_relevant_material: The inferior tribunal failed to consider material relevant to its decision.
predicates.tribunal_relied_on_inadmissible_material: The inferior tribunal relied on material that was not admissible.

issues.definition: When a party challenges an inferior tribunal’s order in supervisory review, the High Court may interfere if the tribunal committed at least one of the specified decision-making errors.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant is habitually in arrears where the tenant repeatedly fails to pay rent by the agreed monthly due date, even if the tenancy terms separately allow notice and a period to settle arrears before termination.
material_facts: The lease required the tenant to pay rent before the tenth day of each calendar month.
The tenant paid the rent for September through November 1984 in December, after a distress warrant had been obtained.
The record also showed further failures to pay rent on the schedule specified in the lease.
The Rent Controller found habitual default, and the Supreme Court upheld that finding under the applicable rent-control ground.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was habitually in arrears because the repeated failures to pay rent by the agreed due date showed continuity of default; the later notice-and-settlement term did not grant an additional four months for paying rent.
issues.legal_principle: Clause 13(3)(ii) of the Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, requires the Controller to be satisfied that the tenant is habitually in arrears. “Habitually” connotes continuity. A tenant who repeatedly fails to meet the monthly rent date may be habitually in arrears even if rent is later paid, including after enforcement steps; a separate term allowing notice and time to settle arrears does not change the monthly payment obligation.

predicates.rent_control_default_proceeding: A rent-control proceeding concerned whether a tenant’s payment conduct amounted to habitual default.
predicates.rent_due_on_fixed_monthly_date: The tenancy required rent to be paid by a specified day in each month.
predicates.tenant_repeatedly_failed_to_pay_by_due_d: The tenant failed on multiple occasions to pay rent by the agreed monthly due date.

issues.definition: In a rent-control proceeding, repeated failure to pay rent by a fixed monthly due date means that the tenant is habitually in arrears.

issues.legal_issue: Subletting is established when a tenant parts with possession of the premises to another in return for consideration.
material_facts: The tenant entered into an agreement with a sewing-machine company described as a consignment dealership.
Under the agreement, the company had exclusive possession of the premises and conducted business there.
The tenant received Rs. 1,500 per month, described as commission, for allowing the company to use the premises.
The Supreme Court held that the agreement’s terms showed that the payment was consideration for parting with possession.
issues.conclusion: The tenant had sublet the premises because the tenant had parted with possession and received consideration for doing so.
issues.legal_principle: To establish subletting under Clause 13(3)(iii) of the Central Provinces and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, both parting with possession and consideration for that parting must be established. The Court corrected the appellate authority’s conclusion because it was based on a misconstruction of the agreement; it did not rely on the earlier cases cited by counsel.

predicates.rent_control_subletting_proceeding: A rent-control proceeding concerned whether a tenant had sublet premises.
predicates.tenant_parted_with_possession: The tenant gave another person possession of the premises.
predicates.tenant_received_consideration_for_posses: The tenant received money or other consideration in return for giving the other person possession.

issues.definition: In a rent-control subletting proceeding, subletting is established when the tenant both gives another person possession and receives consideration for doing so.
